stages.title: Bounded blocking queue
stages.say: Producers and consumers share a buffer of fixed size. Producers block when it is full, consumers when it is empty. Design and build it — and tell me what you would use in production first.
stages.require: Implement `Enqueue`, `TryDequeue`, `Complete`, `Count`. After `Complete`, `Enqueue` throws `InvalidOperationException`; consumers drain, then get false.

stages.title: Cancellation
stages.say: Callers need to be able to give up. A producer is blocked on a full queue and its request is cancelled — what happens?
stages.require: A blocked `Enqueue` or `TryDequeue` must throw `OperationCanceledException` promptly when its token is cancelled.

flaw.ctx: You asked for a bounded blocking queue.
flaw.answer: Two defects. `if` instead of `while`: a woken consumer does not re-check, so two consumers woken for one item both dequeue → exception. `Pulse` with one shared monitor: a producer can wake another producer, and the consumer that needed waking sleeps forever. **Hung or threw in 10 of 10 trials.**
flaw.fix: `while` around every Wait; `PulseAll` (or separate conditions). See BoundedBlockingQueue.

qa.a: Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

qa.q: What does a bounded Channel do when full?
qa.a: Depends on `FullMode`. `Wait`: `WriteAsync` waits, `TryWrite` returns false. `DropWrite/DropNewest/DropOldest`: drops and `TryWrite` returns **true** (R14).

qa.q: When Interlocked instead of a lock?
qa.a: A single-word update with no invariant tying it to other fields — counters. Two fields that must agree need a lock.
SemaphoreSlim can be awaited (`WaitAsync`) and counts beyond 1; it is not re-entrant and must be released in a `finally`.

qa.q: Does async create a new thread?
qa.a: No. `async` lets a method be suspended; `await` on an incomplete task returns to the caller and schedules the rest as a continuation. No thread exists for the waiting.

The OS completes the I/O (I/O completion ports on Windows, epoll on Linux) and the continuation is queued to the thread pool or the captured context. The thread was free the whole time — that is the point.

Cooperatively. You pass a `CancellationToken` down; APIs that accept it observe it and throw `OperationCanceledException`. Nothing is aborted from outside. Blocked primitives need a registration to wake them (BoundedBlockingQueue does this).

qa.q: Can you await inside a lock?
qa.a: No — the compiler forbids it, because the continuation may run on another thread. Use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with `Release` in a `finally` (R12 is what happens without the finally).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: A bounded queue shared by producer and consumer threads: producers block when full, consumers block when empty. Then add cancellation and graceful shutdown.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- `Enqueue` blocks while full
- `TryDequeue` blocks while empty; returns false once completed and drained
- `CancellationToken` on both
- `Complete()` for shutdown

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: In production C# you say `Channel.CreateBounded<T>` and move on. Built by hand, everything rests on two rules: **wait in a `while` loop** (re-check the condition after every wake), and **`PulseAll`** when producers and consumers share one monitor (a `Pulse` can wake the wrong kind of waiter).

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: One `object` gate, a `Queue<T>`, a completed flag. Cancellation registers a callback that pulses the monitor, because `Monitor.Wait` cannot observe a token.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Enqueue: lock; while full and not completed: wait. Throw if cancelled or completed. Enqueue; PulseAll.
- TryDequeue: lock; while empty and not completed: wait. If empty now, return false (completed). Dequeue; PulseAll.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| Queue<T> | FIFO storage |
| Monitor.Wait / PulseAll | Condition waiting inside the lock |
| CancellationToken.Register | Wakes blocked waiters on cancel |
| bool _completed | Shutdown signal; consumers drain then exit |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Enqueue: lock; while full and not completed: wait. Throw if cancelled or completed. Enqueue; PulseAll.
- TryDequeue: lock; while empty and not completed: wait. If empty now, return false (completed). Dequeue; PulseAll.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: O(1) per operation plus waiting. PulseAll wakes every waiter — fine at small thread counts; two condition variables (or SemaphoreSlim pairs) scale better.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- 4 producers × 5,000 items, 4 consumers: sum and count of consumed = produced — nothing lost or duplicated.
- Consumers exit after Complete.
- A producer blocked on a full queue throws on cancellation within 100 ms.
- Enqueue after Complete throws; remaining item drains; then false.

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Bounded blocking queue**

- producers finished (no deadlock)
- consumers exit after Complete
- nothing lost or duplicated (sum)
- nothing lost or duplicated (count)
- enqueue after Complete throws
- drain after Complete
- then false
- capacity 0 rejected

**S2 — Cancellation**

- blocked producer honours cancellation
- promptly (… ms)
- blocked consumer honours cancellation

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Name `Channel<T>` first. Then, if building by hand: ask for the implementation, then ask "where must this use while instead of if, and why?" and check its answer against the code.
- Ask for a stress test that asserts conservation (sum consumed = sum produced), not ordering.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe one Monitor over a Queue<T>, waiting in while-loops and waking with PulseAll, plus a completed flag so consumers can drain and exit — and Channel.CreateBounded<T> is what I would use in production. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Enqueue, TryDequeue and Complete concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: A blocked Enqueue or TryDequeue must throw OperationCanceledException promptly when its token is cancelled. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- `if` instead of `while` around Wait (R9).
- `Pulse` instead of `PulseAll` with one shared monitor (R9) — hung or threw in 10/10 trials.
- Ignoring the cancellation token while blocked.
- No completion signal, so consumers can never exit (the InterviewDB Q15 interface has the same flaw).

**Verification exercise:** Race condition — Two defects. `if` instead of `while`: a woken consumer does not re-check, so two consumers woken for one item both dequeue → exception. `Pulse` with one shared monitor: a producer can wake another producer, and the consumer that needed waking sleeps forever. **Hung or threw in 10 of 10 trials.**

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
This *is* the concurrency question. Answer both: two producers at once — both wait in the loop, each re-checks after waking, so neither overfills. The boundary is the whole operation.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Two producers, queue has one slot.* — Both wait in the while loop; one wins
- *Could this deadlock?* — Not with one monitor and while-loops

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Consumers 10× slower.* — Bounded capacity is back-pressure; block, drop or reject

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Queue depth and producer wait time as metrics.
- A poison item that crashes a consumer: catch per item, dead-letter it, keep the loop alive.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *Shutdown with items in flight.* — Complete, drain with a deadline
- *A poison item.* — Per-item catch, dead-letter

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Implement it.* — While-loop waits, PulseAll.
- *Cancellation.* — Token + registration that pulses.
- *Shutdown.* — Complete(); drain; false.
- *Async.* — `Channel<T>`, or two `SemaphoreSlim`s with `WaitAsync` — never block a thread-pool thread.
- *In production.* — Bounded capacity *is* back-pressure. Metrics: depth, wait time, drops. Decide what happens when full: block, drop oldest, or reject.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Capacity 0? Dequeue after complete? Enqueue after complete?* — Reject; false when drained; throw

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Cost of PulseAll?* — Wakes all waiters — fine small, use two conditions at scale

stages.name: Bounded blocking queue
stages.yours: Three rules, said out loud: producers **block while full**; consumers **block while empty**; after `Complete()`, enqueue throws and consumers **drain, then get false**. One lock, `Monitor.Wait` in **while** loops, `PulseAll`.
stages.ai: **Co-generate**, then let the AI write the 4-producer / 4-consumer stress test.
bad: Implement a blocking queue in C#.
Either a `BlockingCollection` wrapper (fine in production, but it hides the primitive being asked for) or Monitor code with `if` and `Pulse`.
No exclusions, so it uses the library or the shortcut
Nothing about waking the right thread
good: Implement BoundedBlockingQueue<T> below with one private lock and Monitor.Wait/PulseAll. Wait in while loops, never if. Enqueue blocks while full; TryDequeue blocks while empty. After Complete(), Enqueue throws InvalidOperationException and TryDequeue drains what is left, then returns false. Capacity <= 0 throws. No BlockingCollection, no SemaphoreSlim. Keep my fields and signatures. Explain why each Wait sits in a while loop. Show only the class.
**while** and **PulseAll** named — the two known defects excluded
stages.reply: Typical defect (verified planted flaw R9): **`if` instead of `while`** — two consumers woken for one item both dequeue; **`Pulse`** with one shared monitor wakes a producer when a consumer was needed → deadlock.
validate: Every Wait is inside a while that re-checks the condition
PulseAll, because producers and consumers wait on the same lock
Sum and count conserved across 4 producers and 4 consumers
After Complete: drain, then false; Enqueue throws
stages.fix: `if` → `while` and `Pulse` → `PulseAll` are one word each → **by hand**, saying why for each.
stages.say: "While, because a woken thread must re-check — someone may have taken the item first. PulseAll, because producers and consumers share one lock."
stages.require: Implement `Enqueue`, `TryDequeue`, `Complete`, `Count`. After `Complete`, `Enqueue` throws `InvalidOperationException`; consumers drain, then get false.
stages.say_iv: Producers and consumers share a buffer of fixed size. Producers block when it is full, consumers when it is empty. Design and build it — and tell me what you would use in production first.

stages.name: Cancellation
stages.yours: The point to make: a thread **already waiting** will not notice a cancelled token on its own. Something must **wake** it — register a callback that takes the lock and calls PulseAll.
bad: `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` at the top of each method only — a thread already blocked in Wait never wakes.
Passes a test that cancels before calling, fails one that cancels while blocked
good: Add a CancellationToken to Enqueue and TryDequeue. A thread already waiting must wake promptly when the token is cancelled and throw OperationCanceledException: register a callback (ct.Register) that takes the lock and calls PulseAll, and check the token inside the while loop before each Wait. Dispose the registration. Keep my other members unchanged; not a polling loop. Explain how a waiting thread wakes. Show only Enqueue and TryDequeue.
stages.reply: Typical defect: the callback calls PulseAll **without taking the lock** → SynchronizationLockException on the timer thread.
validate: Cancel while blocked: throws within a few hundred ms
The callback takes the lock before PulseAll
Both a blocked producer and a blocked consumer
stages.fix: Missing lock in the callback → **by hand**: wrap it in `lock`.
stages.say: "Checking the token isn't enough — a waiting thread is asleep. The registration wakes it so it can see the cancellation."
stages.require: A blocked `Enqueue` or `TryDequeue` must throw `OperationCanceledException` promptly when its token is cancelled.
stages.say_iv: Callers need to be able to give up. A producer is blocked on a full queue and its request is cancelled — what happens?
